newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German stocks, bonds charge to records.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German stocks, bonds charge to records.

text.p: German bonds and stocks stormed ahead on Tuesday, notching up record highs reflecting a dream scenario of sustained growth with low inflation and low interest rates.

"We have a dream constellation of historically low interest rates, the growth dynamic of companies and large interest from international investors," said Peter Pietsch, economist at Commerzbank. "Things could really not be better."

Germany's DAX index of 30 top shares powered ahead to end at a record bourse high of 2,886.98 points, gaining 28.38 points, or 0.99 percent, after the dollar shot to a 23-month peak overnight, boosting shares in the exporting chemicals and auto sectors in particular.
Germany's DAX has made new records now for four days in a row, gaining three percent, or 89 points, since last Wednesday.

German governent bonds have also raced ahead, with the December Bund future touching an all-time high of 102.99 on Tuesday, as speculation of possible further German rate cuts crept back into the market.
The average current yield on German bonds fell to 5.02 percent, the third historical low in a row.
When economic growth picks up, share and bond markets usually move in opposite directions, stocks gaining and bonds falling on worries of increasing inflation and interest rates.
But the current rally in both bond and stocks reflects hopes for economic recovery without excessive inflation.

The dollar zoomed higher following comments by Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing and New York Federal Reserve Bank William McDonough on the dollar becoming more important in the run up to European monetary union, due in 1999.
Dollar strength and corresponding mark weakness should boost Germany's export-oriented economy, which was held back last year by mark strength.

But despite the boost from a lower dollar, some economists still think there is room for further interest rate cuts to help stimulate the German economy, which has been struggling to come out of a prolonged recession.
Data released on Tuesday showed an unexpected fall in pan German October industrial production of 1.8 percent on the previous month which analysts said may be a one-off decline.
But it does increase speculation about an interest rate cut.

"The strong decline in industrial production is a big surprise. The figures will put further pressure on the mark. New speculation of cuts in German interest rates should be expected," said Klaus Baader, analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

Such speculation, which had been all-but dead in Germany, was first revived last week when France monetary policy council member Jean-Pierre Gerard said short-term interest rates should be cut in Germany and France to boost the dollar and help exporters in the two countries.
But other commentators said hopes for a further interest rate cut in Germany were misplaced and the current bond market gains was just a case of the rally feeding the rally.
"The Bundesbank cannot just lower interest rates because some people abroad and in Germany want that. Rate cuts must have a fundamental basis, which I do not see," said Commerzbank's Pietsch.

The Bundesbank on Tuesday declined to comment directly on rate cut talk in the market, but drew attention to earlier comments by its president Hans Tietmeyer that rates would remain steady in the short term.
